analysis.one_liner: Requires microbe testing of meat and poultry, warnings on raw meat labels, and cleanliness rules for processing plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and two of its subcommittees in April 1993 and sat there until the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the Department of Agriculture to test a statistically significant sample of meat and poultry carcasses for dangerous bacteria like E. coli and Salmonella, set legal limits on how much contamination a product could carry, and condemn and destroy products that exceeded those limits. It would have required warning labels and safe handling and cooking instructions on all raw meat and poultry sold in stores or served in restaurants, applied the same testing rules to imported meat and poultry, and required recordkeeping so contaminated products could be traced back to their source. The meat and poultry industry would have paid fees covering the full cost of the new testing, research, and labeling programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who buys and eats meat and poultry. Microbial testing with enforceable limits, plant cleanliness standards, traceability records, and warning labels would reduce the chance that bacteria invisible to the eye — the kind that caused deadly E. coli and Salmonella outbreaks — reach American kitchens and restaurant plates. Imported products would have to meet the same standard as domestic ones.

how_it_helps.text: Adds dangerous bacteria levels to the legal definition of adulterated meat and poultry, and requires microbial testing of a statistically significant sample of carcasses and products to find them [S2] [S3].

Products testing above the allowed pathogen level would be stamped 'Inspected and condemned' and destroyed, and plants that failed to condemn or destroy contaminated product could lose their inspectors [S3].
Requires warning labels plus handling and cooking instructions on all raw meat and poultry sold at retail or served in restaurants, with unlabeled products deemed misbranded [S2] [S3].

Applies the same pathogen testing requirements to imported meat and poultry, and requires recordkeeping adequate to trace contaminated product back to its source, including an animal identification program [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors and importers. They would pay fees designed to cover the entire cost of the microbial testing, labeling, research, and animal identification programs each year, and they would bear the cost of condemned product, plant cleanliness upgrades, and new recordkeeping. Some of those costs would likely be passed to shoppers as somewhat higher meat prices; the bill's premise is that the price of preventing food poisoning is worth it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Meat and poultry processors and importers

drawbacks.text: The fee structure under Section 305 would collect an amount equal to total annual appropriations for these programs from inspected establishments, so testing and compliance costs would fall on processors first and likely reach consumers as higher meat prices [S3].

Small slaughterhouses and processors would bear the same recordkeeping, labeling, and fee obligations as large ones, and raw meat and poultry can carry some bacteria even when produced correctly, so enforceable pathogen limits could condemn product that careful handling at home would have made safe.

Requiring pathogen limits on raw products was an aggressive standard at the time; the industry's good-faith objection was that meat is cooked before eating and that consumer education and cooking instructions could manage the risk without testing every category of product.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is large and the bill is carefully designed: it sets limits through a rulemaking process based on collected science, covers imports equally, and makes the industry — not general taxpayers — pay the program's cost through fees. The main costs are higher compliance expenses for processors, likely partly passed to shoppers, and heavier paperwork for small plants. On balance the protections clearly outweigh those costs; the bill was never seriously tested because it never received a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to two subcommittees, and no markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Kreidler introduced the Food-borne Illness Prevention Act of 1993 on April 21, 1993, with Rep. Al Swift as the original cosponsor, and it was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture [S1] [S3] [S5].
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Department Operations and Nutrition and the Subcommittee on Livestock, where it stayed [S5].

The bill drew 11 cosponsors — 10 Democrats and 1 Republican — but the Agriculture Committee never reported it out, and no vote was ever taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors and importers came out ahead: by the bill dying in subcommittee, they avoided microbial testing, pathogen limits, condemnation of contaminated product, traceability records, and industry-paid fees for at least the remainder of that Congress. Shoppers got no new federal protection against bacterial contamination from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and poultry processors and importers

for.name: Rep. Mike Kreidler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 10 House Democrats and 1 House Republican
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, for a total of 11 cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair E. de la Garza)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never reported it out or scheduled a markup during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Meat and poultry processing industry
against.role: Subject of the bill's testing, labeling, fee, and condemnation requirements
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory pathogen testing and standards on raw meat and poultry, the position the bill sought to overcome.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was nearly unanimous-D with one Republican cosponsor (11 total: 10 D, 1 R), but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required microbial testing of their products, allowed pathogen levels they could be condemned for exceeding, plant cleanliness standards, traceability records, and annual fees covering the full cost of the program. Their interest in avoiding those costs ran directly against the public's interest in uncontaminated meat.
Imported meat and poultry would have had to participate in the same microbial testing program and meet the same pathogen levels as domestic product, closing a gap in the existing inspection regime.

They would have had to carry warning labels and safe-handling and cooking instructions on raw meat and poultry, a modest compliance cost, while the labels helped protect their customers from mishandling contaminated product at home.
